The word nom ( S. dharma) acquired a very special meaning as a philosophical term by designating the irreducible elements for the construction of a pluralistic world conception comprising botli external and internal phenomena. There are various attemps at rendering this term in English, such as 'element, ''essence', 'mental dates', 'mentals', none of them is quite satisfactory. Datum pl. data, might perhaps be acceptable, if one ignores the fact that a datum, by its very etymology, presupposes a subject. examples.def: T. lhan cig (tu) byung ba; S. sahaja. Born simultaneously, coexistent. Especially applied to a genius protector supposed to be born and existing simultaneously with an exalted person, such as the Bu. and charged with accompanying him through all his life, according to popular belief. In India this belief was extended even to the certain exclusive possessions of such a person. Legend gave a genius protector also to Sagjamuni. Here he was later identified with Vacirbani (see γar tegen vacirtu). For the objects co-existent with the Bu. see erdeni, dolu) an. def: T. rdo rje; S. vajra. Thunderbolt; diamond; the all-destroying, indestructible weapon of Xormusda (Indra) was early used metaphorically to suggest immutability, permanency, and the like. In late Buddhism it became the symbol of the absolute. See kølgen and bej-e. In the mystical sphere it assumed connotations of the linga (phallus) in Hinduism, its counterpart (the yoni) being the xongxu. As a ritualist implement it may have developed out of the serege. The vacir, made of metal, 4-5 inches long, resembles an open-worked dumbell . It and the xongxu symbolize the male deity and its female counterpart (T. nus pa, S. cakti).
